source.title: Antipodes of Label Differential Privacy: PATE and ALIBI
source.authors: Mani Malek; Ilya Mironov; Karthik Prasad; I. Shilov; Florian Tramèr

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including supplemental sections.
record.tranche_reason: Measures models’ memorization of deliberately mislabeled canaries using a black-box attack, a different measure of label memorization than the claim’s training-error test.
record.gate_note: The paper inserts mislabeled canaries and reports attack-based empirical privacy-loss estimates. It does not report training error on fully random labels, test error at chance, or the other claim-version outcomes. Those privacy estimates are recorded as findings about canary memorization, not as measurements of the versions’ stated outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study measures attack-based label privacy for two specialized privacy-preserving training procedures using 1,000 mislabeled canaries. It does not measure any version's random-label fitting, convergence, generalization, regularization, or learning-order outcome. Its citation of the original studies provides background on memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' memorization conclusion: their attack suggests less label memorization by PATE-FM at comparable accuracy, with the reversal of theoretical privacy rankings occurring on CIFAR-100. These attack-based lower bounds remain provisional and do not establish actual privacy rankings against all attacks. The broader conclusion also emphasizes both methods' accuracy/privacy tradeoffs and PATE-FM's much greater computational cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates label-DP training procedures, PATE-FM and ALIBI, then measures canary memorization through a black-box attack; it does not reproduce the original random-label training-error experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and matched accuracy level vary across the reported privacy estimates.

fits_no_version.finding: A confidence-based attack distinguishes inserted canary labels under label-DP training. Its privacy-loss intervals generally favor PATE-FM over ALIBI at comparable test accuracy, particularly on CIFAR-100; some intervals overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these privacy procedures and this attack, label distinguishability can differ substantially despite comparable classification accuracy, and theoretical privacy upper bounds need not rank procedures like empirical attack estimates.

record.problems: The canary attack is a heuristic that inserts many canaries into one model and assumes guesses are independent for its confidence estimates. The authors note that the attack may not be strongest possible and omit multiple-hypothesis corrections. The paper does not measure the claim versions’ training-error or generalization outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 reports a validation of the multiple-canary heuristic for ALIBI (single run with N=1000 versus ten runs with N=100), and Table 6 compares ALIBI with AGIBI. Omitted because these report validation/comparison of the attack or privacy mechanisms, not additional outcomes for the claim versions or the canary-memorization comparison recorded above.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on a completely random labeling, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases. The reported computational comparison is between privacy procedures.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a label-corruption sweep.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it impairs true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels; no training-trajectory comparison is reported.

record.verdict_notes: Canary distinguishability is conditional on the attack's confidence threshold and compares two incorrect candidate labels; it is not training accuracy on the assigned random labels. All rows belong under fits_no_version rather than as evidence for V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training error on completely random labels or test error at chance under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Does not compare training time for true versus random labels or report convergence as label corruption rises.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not sweep the fraction of randomly corrupted labels or report training and test error across such a sweep.
Does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Does not compare learning of real-data patterns with later memorization of noisy labels over training.
